course_description:
This course explores the cutting edge of recent and contemporary philosophy and how it relates to earlier philosophical traditions. The course will draw from the history of philosophy to address current issues. Topics will be drawn from questions in Epistemology and Metaphysics, Logic, European Philosophy and Moral and Political Philosophy.

This course is arranged around three independent modules each examining the application of philosophical methods or concepts to contemporary problems.

Module 1: This module considers the relationship between critical and creative thinking, leadership, strategic planning, decision-making, and organisational culture.

Module 2 : This module considers how AI reshapes human autonomy, agency, relationships, and flourishing when autonomy is understood as relational rather purely individual.

Module 3: This module explores the social contexts of reasoning and evaluates existing reasoning structures according to the principle s of concepts of effective collaborative reasoniing.

assessment_details.task_description: Strategic design thinking challenge: Having recently graduated from university, you are employed as a new member of a community engagement team for a not-for-profit (NFP) organisation. As part of the team, you have been tasked with designing a new philanthropic campaign that will help to diversify the income base of the organisation. You're informed that the bulk of donations currently come from traditional fundraising activities, such as gala dinners, silent auctions, one-off donations around the end-of-financial year, and corporate sponsorship. Donations are declining, however, and the number of donors, many of whom are Baby Boomers, is also droppping. The CEO of the NFP hired you because of your philosophical training, which, she believes, could help inject new ideas for a campaign--philosophers are supposed to be able to think outside the box, right?-- help justify the new campaign to stakeholders according to sound philosophical and ethical principles, and attract younger donors. She wants, she says, to improve on the 'relationship marketing' approach that has dominated the organisation and which, she fears, lacks authenticity. But the head of the Community Engagement division takes a very transactional approach to philanthropy, basing his decisions on data on what's worked to bring in donations in the past. He says he is open to hearing alternative proposals, however. As a result, he has divided the division into teams of four to design new campaign ideas that aim to (a) attract engagement by younger donors and (b) satisfy the CEO and stakeholders by being grounded in sound philosophical and ethical reasoning. This assignment involves both teamwork, as befitting strategic design and planning in organisational contexts, and individual assessment. Teams will be required to delegate tasks to individual members and document individual contributions. At the start of the course, students will generate a Team Charter and Peer and Self Evaluation Form to ensure equal contributions, effective communication, and respectful disagreement resolution processes. Capturing the process of developing the proposal for a new campaign is part of your assessment task. This is a 3-part project. Compile all 3 elements and submit together along with the AI declaration coversheet. Part A: Design process and Decision Log (In-class groupwork = 5%. 450 words) Teams of 4 choose or invent a NFP (existing charities can be explored via https://www.acnc.gov.au/charity/programs/map or internet searches; UQ is a registered charity and NFP so you can use UQ if you like). Learn as much as you can about the organisation, its mission and vision, and its impact, and how it uses its philanthropic funding. In tutorials, work together to create a systems map of the problem space, identify leverage points, and design a new campaign. Construct a decision log to capture the group's reasoning process in developing the campaign. Each student submits the same decision log to Turnitin appended to their reflective essay. Teams will present their ideas in their tutorials for feedback in week 4. Teams construct and submit Team Charter and Peer and Self Evaluation templates and submit to the course tutor in week 1. Complete the Peer and Self Evaluation form at the end of the module, append it to the reflective essay and submit together by the due date. See Blackboard site for Decision Log, Team Charter, and Peer and Self Evaluation template examples. Part B: Reflective Essay (Individual assignment = 25%. 1000 words.) Students compose a reflective essay of the group's philanthropic campaign design, justifying the design by reference to philosophical principles and stress testing it against other principled design choices that could have been made. How is the campaign likely to impact and engage stakeholders, particularly, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities? Identify potential risks and benefits and explain why, all things considered, your group decided to opt for this campaign proposal over plausible alternatives. Reflective essays must show evidence of using concepts and principles from the strategic thinking skillset (systems, strategic, entrepreneurial, design, and futures thinking) as well as philosophical and ethical principles. They must also consider what sort of leadership is optimal for creating a culture for curiosity and innovation in NFP organisations aiming to make the world a better place. Part C: Peer and Self Evaluation form (hurdle requirement) (100 words) Each member of the team is required to complete and submit a Peer and Self Evaluation form documenting their own contributions and those of other team members to the strategic design process. Additional information: Students must complete the coversheet declaring any use of Generative AI tools and attach it to the front of the reflective essay and append the Decision Log and Peer and Self Evaluation form to the essay. Consult the Strategic Design Task Sheet under Blackboard for more detail about these tasks. Note on AI: This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. Whilst students may use AI and/or MT technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which artificial intelligence will provide only limited support and guidance. This assessment item is semi-secure. The decision log is created in class and as a group project. For the remainder of this assessment you can use resources such as your notes, course materials, and other tools, including AI, while completing the task. The focus is not on memorising information, but on understanding, applying judgement, and demonstrating your own thinking. Academic Misconduct: Referencing Fabrication or misrepresentation of sources is considered a breach of academic integrity and may be referred for academic misconduct, regardless of performance in other criteria. This includes but is not limited to: citing non-existent sources, attributing false quotes to real sources, or not including accurate page numbers. Criteria and Marking: See Philosophy Criteria Rubric attached under 'Course Files' for more information about the grading criteria and standards. Your assignment will be assessed according to the following criteria: 1. Ability to construct a well-reasoned and justified design. 2. Depth and breadth of knowledge and understanding of the problem space and relevant theories. 3. Ability to work collaboratively to make well-reasoned decisions. 4. Engagement with relevant, significant and credible academic sources and evidence. 5. Insight and/or creativity in interpreting texts or constructing a point of view or argument. 6. Capacity to produce coherent and well-written assignments using correct grammar and syntax. 7. Appropriately referenced, as per APA7 (or other standard referencing system) conventions. Academic Misconduct: Referencing Fabrication or misrepresentation of sources is considered a breach of academic integrity and may be referred for academic misconduct, regardless of performance in other criteria. This includes but is not limited to: citing non-existent sources, attributing false quotes to real sources, or not including accurate page numbers. Criteria and Marking: See Philosophy Criteria Rubric attached under 'Course Files' for more information about the grading criteria and standards. Your assignment will be assessed according to the following criteria: 1. Ability to construct a well-reasoned and justified design. 2. Engagement with relevant, significant and credible academic sources and evidence. 5. Insight and/or creativity in interpreting texts or constructing a point of view or argument. 6. Capacity to produce coherent and well-written assignments using correct grammar and syntax. 7. Appropriately referenced, as per APA7 (or other standard referencing system) conventions. learning_activities.topic: Week 1: Course Introduction and Entrepreneurial Design Thinking This week provides an overview of the course and introduces students to the basics of entrepreneurial and design thinking and what philosophy has to do with all that. Students form into teams for teamwork projects, design Team Charter and Peer and Self Evaluation forms, and select or design their organisation for the design challenge. Learning outcomes: L01, L05, L06

Week 2: Systems thinking and mapping This week introduces philosophical principles of systems thinking and its role in strategic thinking and planning. Tutorials commence. Students produce a systems map of the problem they are endeavouring to address in their design challenge. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L06, L07

Week 3: Strategic thinking and futures thinking. The week covers strategic decision-making, situational thinking, strategic thinking and intelligence, and futures thinking. In tutorials, students develop arguments for their campaign stress testing it against other plausible options.

Week 4: Discursive leadership Is there such a thing as leading philosophically? This seminar explores the principles of discursive leadership and the contribution that philosophical skills and concepts can make to creating positive workplace cultures and cultures that support ideation and innovation. In tutorials, representatives from each group pitch the ideas for their campaigns and stress test them against critical feedback from their classmates. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L06, L07

Week 5: From individual to relational autonomy The aim of this module is to examine AI through the lens of relational autonomy. In this seminar we consider what relational autonomy is and how it differs from traditional conceptions of autonomy, and we ask why relational autonomy is especially relevant for understanding and assessing AI-mediated societies. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L06

Week 6: Algorithmic shaping of choice and agency This seminar considers how AI systems influence decision-making and self-formation, and analyses AI-mediated decision processes to identify sources of influence and manipulation, forms of dependency, and opportunities for resistance and reflection. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L06

Week 7: Relational autonomy, power, and AI systems This seminar examines how AI systems reshape social relationships, social power, and conditions for autonomy. We consider social dependency and technological mediation, algorithmic bias and structural injustice, recognition and identity formation, and trust and authority in the context of human-AI relationships. In class critical reflection during week 7 tutorials (see assessment). Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L05, L06

Week 8: AI and human flourishing This seminar reflects on what capacities are essential for flourishing, and whether AI can enhance flourishing without undermining relational autonomy. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L06, L07

Week 9: Collaborative reasoning I This section examines evidence that reason is best understood as a social competence evolved for optimising social situations. many of the aspects of our reasoning that seem unusual if viewed as an individual capacity make more sense through a social lens. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L06, L07

Week 10: Collaborative reasoning II This session considers models of reasoning and how it develops. We consider concepts of knowledge construction, expertise, and dual process reasoning and how they interplay to develop a working understand of developing reasoning. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L06

Week 11: Collaborative reasoning III This section considers some of the problems of social thinking, including groupthink, and explores solutions and alternative methods of social collaboration. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06, L07

Week 12: Collaborative reasoning IV In this session students will discuss the material covered and how it relates to a range of collaborative contexts. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06, L07
Review Week No classes this week. Students are encouraged to use this time to prepare their final assesment with course lecturers available for consultation.
